newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bonino's food safety "bible" to be adopted on Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Bonino's food safety "bible" to be adopted on Wednesday.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to approve a report on Wednesday laying down guidelines for food safety controls and the use of scientific advisers, Commission officials said.
They said the guidelines amount to a bible for the new food safety commissioner Emma Bonino as she seeks to reassure consumers shaken by health scares over mad cow disease and E-coli bacteria.
But the report had to be substantially redrafted after fierce criticism from farm commissioner Franz Fischler and others who lost substantial powers in the reorganisation.
In addition to agriculture, the industry, health, internal market and research DGs are also affected.
The shake-up follows a pledge by Commission president Jacques Santer to the European Parliament on February 18 to give priority to protecting consumer health and guaranteeing food safety.
Santer's pledge helped to persuade the parliament to postpone a possible censure motion for mishandling the mad cow crisis until November.
"It's the start of a European model for food safety," said one official, adding it was a broader-based equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
The EU model is more comprehensive because it covers meat, poultry and fish which are outside the FDA's jurisdiction.
The model is based on the separation of powers and widest possible distribution of information on food safety.
Firstly, responsibility for food legislation and scientific advice will be separated as will control of legislation and inspection of food safety standards.
Previously Fischler and the directorate general for agriculture DG VI were responsible for drafting agricultural rules as well as enforcing them.
Industry commissioner Martin Bangemann was mainly responsible for drawing up rules for the food industry.
Under the new system, seven scientific committees will advise Bonino on food safety.
The committees, which previously reported to Fischler, have been criticised for being inefficient, lacking independence from national governments and for excessive secrecy.
The watchwords now are "excellence, independence and transparency", said an official.
Regarding food safety inspections, risk assessments will be carried out to set priorities. National food control systems will also be scrutinised.
Inspections will be conducted throughout the food production chain from the "plough to the plate" to prevent any food safety gaps.
But officials stressed that Bonino must be given the financial resources to carry out the job.

"The hour of truth is approaching," said one official, saying that funds were needed to take on an extra 166 food safety inspectors and other experts, of which 97 would have to be recruited from outside the Commission.
